system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2204-08-30 18:28:00 to 2204-09-07 14:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with multiple sclerosis and a chronic indwelling Foley catheter, was admitted with fever and fatigue due to sepsis. The infection source was determined to be a combination of a severely infected stage IV sacral pressure ulcer with underlying osteomyelitis and a urinary tract infection. He underwent surgical debridement of the ulcer and was started on intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. Blood cultures revealed skin flora, supporting a wound origin, and he improved clinically with normalization of inflammatory markers. A PICC line was placed for six weeks of outpatient antibiotic therapy. He was discharged to an extended care facility for wound care and rehabilitation, with plans to follow up with infectious disease and urology, the latter to discuss suprapubic catheter placement given recurrent urosepsis. Nutritional support and mental health resources were also arranged.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter

INDICATION:  ___ year old man admitted with gram negative bacteremia, will need

Dr. ___ (interventional radiology attending) performed the procedure.
The attending was present and supervising throughout the procedure.

ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.

CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 0.4 min, 1 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Double lumen PICC placement through the basilic vein on the
left.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, multiple
attempts were made to access the right basilic vein, however, all were
unsuccessful due to small caliber and tortuosity. The cephalic vein and
brachial vein on the right were not adequate for PICC insertion.

At this time the left upper extremity was prepped and draped in usual sterile
fashion. The basilic vein on the left was punctured under direct ultrasound
guidance using a micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained
before and after intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away
sheath was then placed over a guidewire. The guidewire was then advanced into
the superior vena cava using fluoroscopic guidance. A double lumen PIC line
measuring 39 cm in length was then placed through the peel-away sheath with
its tip positioned in the distal SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. Position of
the catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The
peel-away sheath and guidewire were then removed. The catheter was secured to
the skin, flushed, and a sterile dressing applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1. The accessed vein was patent and compressible.

2. Basilicvein approach double lumen left PICC with tip in the distal SVC.

3. Failed right upper extemity venous access attempts

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a left 39 cm basilic approach double lumen PICC with
tip in the distal SVC. The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re in the hospital now. You were brought in because you were weak and your blood pressure was low. Do you remember what happened this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I was at the nursing home. I felt dizzy, sweaty. I think it’s my bladder again. Like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your urine showed signs of infection, and your white blood cell count is very high. We think you have a urinary tract infection that’s spread into your blood—this is called sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sepsis? That sounds serious. Am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we caught it early. You’re in the ICU for close monitoring. We’ve started antibiotics and fluids. Your blood pressure dropped, so we gave you medication to support it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… thank you. My catheter was blocked, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The CT scan showed your bladder was very full—hydronephrosis, meaning your kidneys were backing up. The catheter was stuck in your prostate. Urology repositioned it, and you passed over a liter of urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had trouble with that before. The hole at the base of my penis… it’s not healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. There’s an erosion where the catheter goes in. It’s not actively infected, but it’s a concern. We’ll follow up with urology after you’re better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this catheter for years. Maybe it’s time for a change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking the same thing. A suprapubic catheter might be better to avoid this kind of issue. We’ll discuss it with your urologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my ostomy—my bowel keeps coming out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the surgery team saw you. They reduced the prolapse manually. But since it’s happened more than once, they recommend fixing it surgically when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. It’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it’s on your follow-up plan. For now, focus on getting through this infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure is stable, and you’re off the pressors. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My breathing feels better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chest X-ray showed some fluid buildup from the fluids we gave you, but it’s clearing. No pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? My creatinine was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your kidney function was affected—acute kidney injury. Likely from the low blood pressure and the blockage. But it’s improving. Creatinine is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you won’t need it. Your kidneys are recovering. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection? Did they find what it is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Blood and urine cultures grew Proteus mirabilis. It’s a bacteria that can cause UTIs, especially with catheters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the antibiotic working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The bacteria is sensitive to the piperacillin-tazobactam you’re on. We’ll switch to ceftriaxone later for a two-week course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll need that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll place a PICC line for IV antibiotics. You’ll get them at home with nursing support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you to the regular floor today. You’re doing well—afebrile, stable vitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Feels good to be out of ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down from 51,000 to 15,000. Lactate normalized. Kidney function improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pressure sores?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re chronic but not infected. We’re keeping them clean and turning you regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another osteomyelitis like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that now. We’re vigilant about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest chest X-ray shows improvement. No fluid overload now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Breathing easier. Any update on the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for tomorrow. Left arm, basilic vein. Should go smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my baclofen pump? It needs a refill soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted it. Your neurologist will refill it after discharge. We’ll coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your urine culture today is clear. No bacteria. The antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. And blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Negative after the first day. That means the bloodstream infection is clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aiming for early next week. We need to start the PICC antibiotics and make sure everything’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the PICC placement yesterday. Line is in good position. We’ll start ceftriaxone tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any pain or risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Minimal. Just keep the site clean. Nursing will teach you and your sister how to care for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s my healthcare proxy. She’ll help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll go over all the discharge plans with both of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. Your bladder is draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. No more blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. But we still recommend the suprapubic catheter to prevent this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I agree. Let’s do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re almost ready. Final labs show your kidney function is stable, infection markers normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get ceftriaxone daily for two more weeks through the PICC. Home health will assist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urology for the suprapubic catheter, surgery for the ostomy repair, neurology for your pump refill, and infectious disease to wrap up the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you’re cleared to go home. We’ll send all instructions to your sister and your providers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Stay on the antibiotics, keep the PICC clean, and call if you develop fever or redness at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see the specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, Mr. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with advanced multiple sclerosis and a chronic indwelling Foley catheter, was admitted with weakness and hypotension due to septic shock from a Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infection and bacteremia. He presented with a distended bladder and hydronephrosis due to catheter malposition, which was corrected in the emergency department. He required brief vasopressor support and was treated with intravenous antibiotics, transitioning from piperacillin-tazobactam to ceftriaxone after culture results. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic therapy. Acute kidney injury improved with supportive care. Complications included a penile erosion from long-term catheter use and recurrent ostomy prolapse, both addressed with surgical and urological follow-up plans. He stabilized over eight days and was discharged home with services for continued IV antibiotics and specialist appointments.
